"Earthly" means belonging to the Earth or to life on Earth. But the word is flexible — what you contrast "earthly" things against changes its exact meaning. There are two distinct uses, and understanding each one fully is the key to mastering this word.
Meaning 1: Of or relating to life on this Earth — especially as opposed to heaven, the spiritual, or the eternal

This is the most common and important use. When something is described as "earthly," it belongs to the physical, material world we live in — things of this life, this body, this world — as opposed to something divine, heavenly, or eternal.

The implied contrast is always:

Earth ↔ Heaven | Body ↔ Spirit | This life ↔ Afterlife | Material ↔ Spiritual

Think of it this way: if something is "earthly," it is real and physical, it belongs to the here and now, and it will not last forever. It is not divine. It is not spiritual. It is of this world.

Examples:

  • "She gave up all her earthly possessions when she became a nun."

Here, "earthly possessions" means her material belongings — money, clothes, property — the things that belong to life in this world, not to a spiritual life.

  • "He had no interest in earthly pleasures like wealth or fame."

He wasn't drawn to the enjoyments of this material world.

  • "In many religions, earthly life is seen as a brief journey, and the real reward comes after."

"Earthly life" = the physical life we live on this planet, contrasted with an eternal afterlife.

  • "No earthly king rules forever."

No king in this physical world is permanent — unlike a divine or eternal ruler.

This sense appears frequently in religious, philosophical, and literary contexts. But you'll also see it in everyday speech whenever someone contrasts the material world with something bigger, higher, or more permanent.

A natural extension of this meaning: "Earthly" can also simply mean "of the planet Earth" in a more literal, scientific sense — especially when contrasting Earth with space or other worlds.

  • "No earthly creature could survive the temperatures on Venus."
  • "The astronauts deeply missed the earthly sounds of wind and rain."

This is the same core idea — belonging to Earth — just applied more literally and without the spiritual contrast.
Meaning 2: Possible or conceivable — used ONLY in negative sentences or questions (an intensifier)

This is a very different use, and it trips up many learners. Here, "earthly" has nothing to do with the planet or spirituality. Instead, it acts as an intensifying word — it makes a negative statement far stronger by emphasizing that something is completely impossible, pointless, or beyond imagination.

The critical rule: This meaning only works in negative sentences or genuine questions. You cannot say "There is an earthly reason" — it sounds wrong and unnatural. You must say "There is no earthly reason" or "What earthly reason is there?"

Examples:

  • "There is no earthly reason to be afraid."

Not just "no reason" — absolutely, completely, conceivably no reason. "Earthly" makes the denial total.

  • "What earthly use is this broken machine?"

What possible use could it have? (The speaker clearly thinks: none.)

  • "I have no earthly idea what she meant."

I have absolutely, completely no idea. It's a strong, emphatic way of saying "I don't know at all."

  • "There's no earthly way he finished that in ten minutes."

It is completely and utterly impossible that he finished that fast.

In this use, "earthly" is virtually interchangeable with "possible" or "conceivable":

  • No earthly reason ≈ No possible reason ≈ No reason on earth
  • What earthly use? ≈ What possible use?

The tone here is often one of frustration, disbelief, or strong dismissal.

Several words are close neighbors of "earthly," and knowing the differences will sharpen your understanding.

Worldly — also means "of this world," but it focuses specifically on experience, sophistication, and knowledge of how the social and material world works. A "worldly" person is experienced and savvy. "Earthly" carries no such sense of experience or sophistication.

  • "She was a worldly woman who had lived in six countries." (experienced, street-smart)
  • "She renounced her earthly belongings." (the physical things of this world)

Terrestrial — this is the formal, scientific version of "earthly." It refers to the Earth as a planet, especially in contrast to space, water, or other planets. You would not use "terrestrial" in spiritual or emotional contexts.

  • "Terrestrial planets" (Earth-like planets) vs. gas giants — this is science.
  • You say "earthly pleasures" (spiritual contrast), not "terrestrial pleasures" — that would sound cold and strange.

Mortal — means "subject to death." It overlaps with the first sense of "earthly" because both refer to the temporary nature of human life. But "mortal" specifically highlights death, while "earthly" highlights being in the physical world.

Temporal — means "of this life or time, not eternal." Very close to the first sense of "earthly" and often interchangeable in religious or philosophical writing, but it is considerably more formal and stiff-sounding in everyday use.
Words and Phrases Commonly Paired with "Earthly"

These are the collocations — the natural pairings — you will encounter most often:

In the first meaning: earthly possessions, earthly pleasures, earthly life, earthly existence, earthly paradise (a place so beautiful it seems like heaven on Earth), earthly realm, earthly affairs, earthly concerns, earthly body.

In the second meaning: no earthly reason, no earthly idea, no earthly use, no earthly good, no earthly chance, what earthly purpose, what earthly difference.

The first meaning fits comfortably in formal writing, literature, religious texts, philosophy, and equally in casual, reflective conversation. It often carries a slightly serious or thoughtful tone — the feeling that something bigger than everyday life is being considered.

The second meaning is informal and conversational. It adds a punch of emphasis and often carries a note of frustration, exasperation, or strong disbelief. You'd say it to a friend, not write it in an academic essay.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

If you see "earthly" describing things, life, pleasures, possessions, or existence — it means those things belong to the physical, material world of human life, usually contrasted with something spiritual, divine, or eternal.

If you see "earthly" in a negative sentence or a question — paired with words like no, not, what, any — it is an intensifier meaning possible or conceivable, used to make a strong, emphatic point that something is completely out of the question or utterly unknown.
